data.title: These 7 of 11 Democrats vote no on Jeffries for House speaker
data.description:
A bloc of seven incoming House Democrats publicly voted no on Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for Speaker of the House.

Jeffries’s bid was supported by 251 lawmakers, with a total of 11 voting ‘no’ on his promotion to House Speaker. 

The seven who voted against Jeffries are composed of Democratic Rep.-elects Darializa Avila Chevalier (N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (N.J.), Frederick Haynes (Texas), Melat Kiros (Colo.), Donavan McKinney (Mich.), Chris Rabb (Pa.) and Claire Valdez (N.Y.).

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the group wrote in a statement, according to Punchbowl’s Ally Mutnick. 

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations,” they continued. “While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership.”

“Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no,” the bloc concluded.

DSA affiliations

Avila Chevalier, Kiros, McKinney, Rabb and Valdez’s bids to the lower chamber were all backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) which made waves this election cycle for its progressive stances.

Newly elected DSA lawmakers were expected to create headaches for Jeffries as the group reportedly remained divided on how to approach changing the Democratic party’s stances. They’ve hammered their own party for what they see as an abandonment of progressive ideals and a soft-glove approach to President Trump’s second term. 

Kiros’s race in Colorado drew national attention after she ousted 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.). She ran on securing universal childcare and eldercare and supported an ultramillionaire tax on people with a net worth of more than $50 million.

Others in the group ran on similar platforms, overthrowing long-term centrist incumbents.

Nomiki Konst, a progressive strategist who is an inactive member of the DSA, predicted in October that most of the left in the caucus are going to side with Jeffries, noting Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s (D-N.Y.) struggles against then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.)

The new DSA congressional members “have learned the lessons” of Ocasio-Cortez, Konst told The Hill.

Still their lack of support marks a new challenge that Jeffries will be expected to handle as division between centrists and progressives within the party continues to grow. 

Non-DSA progressives

Hamawy and Haynes are not affiliated or a part of the DSA but campaigned on progressive platforms.

Haynes is replacing outgoing Rep. Jasmine Crockett’s (D-Texas) open House seat after her failed bid for Texas’s Senate seat. He differed from Crockett who voted to send U.S. military to Israel.

Christ was against genocide and that if “it’s in Gaza, he’s against it,” he told Texas outlet WFAA.

While Hamawy, a doctor and veteran, took hold of outgoing Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman’s (D-N.J.) seat who served in the House since 2015. On the campaign trail, he wouldn’t commit to backing Jeffries, telling the New Jersey Globe that current Democratic leadership is “failing to meet the moment.”

data.title: Ron Johnson: Remark about shutting down Social Security was 'imprecise'
data.description:
Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, said there is “no way to fix” Social Security, calling for it to be shut down, but later clarified that his comments were “imprecise.”

“At this point, there’s really no way to fix Social Security. It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it, you just shut it down and hope that you can recover some of your money,” Johnson said during an appearance on Fox Business.

During a Senate committee hearing to examine Social Security, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) questioned Johnson’s remarks saying, “This is the first time in decades that a senior senator, the chairman of the Budget Committee, said he would rather shut down Social Security than fix it.”

“Social Security does have to evolve to meet the challenges,” Wyden said.

“This proposition of throwing in the towel folks which is what we heard … I think would be a huge mistake,” he added. “I think the American people would say we sent you there to roll up your sleeves and fix the problem not quit on it.”

Johnson responded by saying, “I was talking about Ponzi schemes … imprecise statement I’ll admit but everything I’ve written everything I’ve said clearly I’m not proposing shutting down Social Security.”

Earlier this month, Wyden said there is a “lot of interest” among lawmakers to raise the Social Security payroll tax cap. In 2026, the wage base limit for Social Security taxes $184,500 in income, according to the Internal Revenue Service website.

“The wage base limit is the maximum wage that’s subject to the tax for that year,” the website says. However, for Medicare, the base limit does not exist.

In June, Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) backed raising the Social Security tax cap in a New York Times opinion piece. 

“This is a no-brainer: The wealthiest Americans, who have benefited the most from America’s opportunities, should contribute the same percentage of their income as a factory worker in Chillicothe, Ohio, or a teacher in Worcester, Mass.,” they wrote.

data.title: Buttigieg on Duffy's Biden administration jabs: 'What the hell is he talking about?'
data.description:
Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg fired back at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy after he blamed the Biden administration for failing to invest in the nation’s aging air traffic control system following last week’s nationwide ground stop.

“What the hell is he talking about? I mean, we launched the biggest infrastructure investment since the Eisenhower years,” Buttigieg said in an interview with MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday.

Buttigieg was responding to comments Duffy made on Fox News, in which the current transportation secretary accused the previous administration of prioritizing changes to aviation terminology and diversity over upgrades to critical infrastructure.

“The last administration wasn’t focused on the infrastructure of aviation,” Duffy said in the clip played during Wednesday’s interview. “They were concerned about what names we use for ‘cockpit.’”

Buttigieg rejected the criticism and questioned why Duffy was seeking an additional $50 billion from Congress.

He touched on how the Trump administration has yet to spend funding already available, including $12.5 billion allocated through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to replace aging infrastructure in the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

“He hasn’t even finished spending some of the funds that we put together in the Biden infrastructure law, nor have they spent, as I understand it, more than about one-tenth of what Congress already gave them in the last budget,” Buttigieg said.

“So they’ve got to explain, the secretary’s got to explain why he has not yet spent more of the resources that have already been given to him,” he continued.

Buttigieg pushed back on Duffy’s critiques of the terminology changes, saying such updates were routine and received little attention during his tenure.

In 2021, the FAA advisory committee released a report advising airlines to shift toward more gender-neutral language in an effort to promote more inclusive language. The group recommended airlines replace words such as “airman” with “aviator” and “cockpit” with “flight deck,” as well as other recommendations.

“I don’t even know if that actually formally crossed my desk,” Buttigieg said of the terminology changes. “He has definitely spent more time on television talking about that than I ever spent.”

data.title: Hegseth meets with Delcy Rodríguez in Venezuela to deepen military partnership
data.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth traveled to Venezuela on Wednesday to meet with Venezuelan acting President Delcy Rodríguez in Caracas, where he announced the U.S. will deepen its military partnership to help counter foreign actors and “narco-terrorists.” 

“We look forward to following through, deepening our defense cooperation and our defense partnership in ways that utilizes the expertise of the U.S. military and the War Department, alongside the great capabilities of your military, to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals, and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders,” the Defense secretary said at the Miraflores Palace. 

The meeting, which was not announced by the Pentagon, was captured by Venezuelan state TV. 

The Pentagon did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. 

The U.S. launched the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (A3C), a military and security initiative, as part of Shield of the Americas, in an effort to combat drug cartels and transnational gangs in the Western Hemisphere. 

Since September last year, the U.S. military has blown up alleged drug trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific. U.S. forces have also interdicted at least eight large boats, which the Pentagon classified as “floating refueling stations,” off the coast of Ecuador. 

The U.S. service members and law enforcement have also embedded with Ecuadorian security forces during raids in September against drug traffickers on the ground. 

Hegseth said the U.S. looks forward to partnering with Venezuela militarily, but also economically. 

“The incredible resource capabilities that your country has that we look forward to unlocking together with you, the prosperity, the peace, the stability of Venezuela means a safer and more secure hemisphere, safer and more secure America, and that partnership demonstrates to the world what’s possible when two great countries, along with a long history, reestablish that partnership together,” Hegseth said while looking at Rodríguez.

On Tuesday, Hegseth was at U.S. Southern Command (Southcom) headquarters in Florida where he met with Southcom commander Gen. Francis Donovan.

Hegseth’s unannounced visit marks another senior Trump administration official visiting Venezuela, after Energy Secretary Chris Wright, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and CIA Director John Ratcliffe did the same. 

The Defense secretary’s trip comes months after the U.S. forces successfully captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and as the Trump administration has brokered a deal to take control of some of the country’s oil reserves. 

Rodríguez said in late August it is a 25-year bilateral project that envisions a development of 17 strategic oil fields, with a goal of producing over 1.5 million barrels per day. 

“Each party contributes what it does best. Venezuela contributes oil, its industry and the experience of its workers accumulated over more than 100 years,” she said at the time. “The United States contributes the capital and technology needed to recover and develop those assets.”

The deal was criticized by some Democrats on Capitol Hill. 

Hegseth’s trip also comes after The New York Times reported earlier this month that the U.S. is in talks with Venezuela to secure a permanent U.S. military presence in the country. 

“We would like to have at some point a presence agreement with them, but largely from a legal standpoint, to make sure that our troops there have legal protections and they’re operating jointly with them,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in an interview with the Times on Nov. 5.

data.title: Unhappy marriages could cause dementia: New study
data.description:
(NewsNation) — New research by the University of Bordeaux, published in the journal Aging & Mental Health, found very lonely people over 65 had a 38 percent risk of developing dementia.

Interestingly, almost a third of those studied (29.5 percent) lived with another person, but said the connection was unfulfilling.

The study looked at 3,777 older adults from 1988 to 2018. The participants self-reported feelings of loneliness and were ranked into three groups: never lonely, occasional loneliness and chronic loneliness. Those who were considered chronically lonely reported loneliness on three to four visits over the course of eight years.

During the second phase, 1,540 participants remained eligible. Almost half of those who fell into the chronic loneliness category developed dementia, at 49 percent. Only 34 percent of those who experienced occasional loneliness and 33 percent of those who were never lonely developed the condition. The results indicate occasional loneliness is not harmful, according to the study.

“The distinction is critical,” senior researcher at the Bordeaux Population Health Center Karine Pérès said in a press release. “While most people experience loneliness at some point in their lives, it is when the loneliness becomes chronic and persistent that it may increase the risk of developing dementia.”

Chronic loneliness triggers inflammation through prolonged activation of stress and immune pathways, according to Pérès. The feeling triggers a “fight or flight” response that increases inflammation and lowers your ability to fight disease. It is also associated with decreased physical activity and poor diet, which contribute to cardiovascular disease and diabetes, both dementia risk factors.

Loneliness is associated with an array of health issues, with research showing that it increases your likelihood of irritable bowel disease, multiple sclerosis, cancer and adds nearly 20 months to your biological age. The new study indicates combating loneliness also involves forming meaningful connections.

“Healthcare professionals, social workers and policymakers should not exclusively focus on living arrangements as a proxy for social risk but should also incorporate subjective experiences of connection and loneliness,” Yvanna Simon, the lead author at the University of Bordeaux, said in a press release.

Researchers say it is important that healthcare workers put a greater emphasis on addressing loneliness in older adults through expanding loneliness screening and referrals to social activities.

data.title: 1 in 5 Trump voters say Republicans will lose White House: Survey
data.description:
Around one in five Trump voters say that Republicans will lose the White House in the next presidential election.

In the Politico poll, 22 percent of respondents that cast their ballot for President Trump in the 2024 election said Democrats will take the White House in 2028. Sixty percent of respondents said a Republican will clinch the presidency in the next election and 18 percent were unsure about which party will be victorious in 2028.

The poll took place shortly after this year’s midterms, in which Democrats won back both the House and Senate.

When it came to all respondents in the Politico poll, 52 percent said they believed Democrats will take the White House in 2028, 28 percent said Republicans will win and 20 percent were unsure.

The midterms were an uphill battle for the Republicans, with the Iran war, Trump’s slumping approval rating and cost of living concerns weighing down the GOP as they went into Election Day.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 37.3 percent as of Wednesday morning, with his disapproval rating at 60.3 percent.

Last Thursday, Trump voiced dissatisfaction with the work of Senate Republicans, calling their actions “devastating” to the GOP and blaming them for their party’s losses in the midterm elections.

“The Republican Senate can no longer be the place ‘where things are sent to die.’ Not passing THE SAVE AMERICA ACT (Voter I.D., Proof of Citizenship), sent up five times by the House, was devastating to the Republican Party in the Midterms,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post.

The Politico poll took place from Nov. 7-10, featuring 2,000 respondents and a margin of error of plus or minus 2 percentage points.

data.title: These bipartisan bills would solve major problems. Why aren't they already law?
data.description:
In an era defined by razor-thin majorities, partisan gridlock, and seemingly endless political battles, finding common ground across the aisle can feel like an impossible task. Yet, despite the dysfunction that often dominates headlines, Congress has shown that bipartisan cooperation is still possible when lawmakers are willing to put politics aside and focus on delivering results for the American people. 

In fact, 13 bipartisan bills offer a promising example of lawmakers working across the aisle to cut through partisan gridlock and advance meaningful policy solutions.

Everyone knows the repair shop at the car dealer rips you off — and customers would be even worse off if drivers could only have their vehicles serviced at the dealer. Yet this is effectively what happens when military equipment is repaired. Many U.S. defense contractors enjoy exclusive rights to repair the military equipment they manufacture. That means even the highly skilled military service members aren’t allowed to fix the mission-critical weapons and equipment they train with every day.

Taxpayers shouldn’t have to pay for exclusive and expensive repairs any more than they should be required to take their car to the dealer every time the check engine light goes on. The Department of Defense should be able to receive technical data necessary to maintain and repair important systems without going back to the manufacturer. 

That’s why the Warrior Right to Repair Act, along with 12 other bills, is on National Taxpayers Union’s 2026 No-Brainer report, a list of legislation with real wins for taxpayers that Congress should take up in its lame-duck session. Even after a divisive midterm election season, it’s safe to say everyone agrees the government should work better and cost taxpayers less. Taxpayers should not be forced to pay for fraud, waste and inefficiency. 

Americans know the frustration of government inefficiency all too well. Just ask any taxpayer who’s ever called the IRS — you’ll hear about long wait times, disputes that don’t get resolved, major technology limitations and the like. The IRS is long overdue for reform.

It’s now within reach through the Taxpayer Assistance and Service Act, awaiting action in the House of Representatives. If the bill passes, taxpayers will be able to see their communication with the IRS and respond online. They’ll know the status of their refunds. They’ll have the option to have a call back instead of waiting on hold for hours. Their ability to challenge IRS decisions would expand, and they’ll enjoy more rights as taxpayers. 

The Senate already approved the bill. The House should take it up immediately before all the progress for taxpayers contained in this bill dies with the new Congress.  

Congress should also make better use of the information the federal government already has available.

The federal government is so big, it’s difficult to keep track of programs already in place. That’s why another no-brainer would be passing the Duplication Scoring Act, which would require review of duplicative or overlapping program proposals. Congress should know if a bill under consideration would recreate another program already in operation. Taxpayers don’t need two of everything.

Meanwhile, the federal government should use tools already in place to fight fraud and improper payment, such as the Department of Treasury’s Do Not Pay system. One of the most common causes of improper payments is a failure to verify recipient and eligibility information before payments are made by the government. Expanding the use of the Do Not Pay system is one of the Government Accountability Office’s top recommendations to combat fraud. Congress should pass the Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act immediately. 

These bills are targeted solutions to real problems that have already been identified. Even though the country seems to be deeply divided, taxpayers, Republicans, Democrats, and independents alike agree the government should work better and safeguard dollars from waste, fraud and abuse. Congress should put these bills and other No-Brainers at the top of its lame-duck agenda.

Thomas Aiello is vice president of federal affairs at National Taxpayers Union.

data.title: Education Department touts changes made to student loans, K-12 investments after a year of interagency agreements
data.description:
The Education Department on Wednesday touted changes to major policies such as student loans and education funding that have come as a result of its 14 interagency agreements. 

Over the past year, the Department of Education has made agreements with the Treasury Department, State Department and others to move some its responsibilities and programs out of its purview as President Trump seeks to wind down the entire department.

The announcement provides fresh details of what those agreements have produced, such as the Treasury and Education Department working together to create the Defaulted Loans Support Center. 

The center gives resources to defaulted borrowers to get back into good standing on their payments, with 89 percent of early user feedback saying the new rehabilitation process was easy, according to the department. 

“For too long, Washington measured success by how many rules it wrote rather than how well students were doing,” Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said. “By working together across six federal departments this past year, we have delivered meaningful wins for families — cutting through the red tape that stands in the way of learning, connecting classrooms to careers, and bolstering enforcement of federal law. Congress now has an opportunity to cement these reforms into law and help return education decisions where they belong: with parents, teachers, and local communities.”

The partnership with the Department of Labor, the Trump administration said, led to $425 million in investments “to boost literacy, expand charter school access, support career-connected learning, strengthen teacher preparation, bolster American History and Civics education, and modernize state academic assessments.” 

The interagency agreements have come under fire from opponents who call them confusing and say they do not actually reduce the red tape the administration is aiming to trim.  

In line with Trump and McMahon’s stated goal to abolish the department, the agency has taken drastic steps, such as firing half of its workforce.  

But to completely shut the doors of the Education Department would take an act of Congress, an idea that stands no chance after Democrats’ victories in this month’s midterm elections.  

Opponents argue the department began the interagency agreements as a way to circumvent that roadblock and further weaken itself. 

Democrats have promised investigations into the agreements after they retake the House and Senate, with mounting concerns over issues such as the number of unresolved civil rights investigations. 

In the Wednesday announcement, the Education Department said the Office of Civil Rights partnership with the Department of Justice has “streamlined the complaint resolution process” and has created more effective enforcement. 

It also highlighted the partnership with the Department of Health and Human Services and emphasized that the Education Department is still the head of oversight for programs with students with disabilities and all funding allocations reached states on time.  

The two agencies also gave 40 new grants totaling $71 million to low-income college parents to access child care. 

“President Trump and Secretary McMahon are cutting red tape and putting families first,” said Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. “HHS is helping strengthen services for students with disabilities, expand affordable child care for parents earning degrees, and support early learning. We’re making federal agencies work together to deliver for American families.”  

Other progress the Education Department highlighted included strengthening tribal relations, grants to employment-focused programs and protecting student privacy.

data.title: Pence: Lutnick 'may need to go'
data.description:
Former Vice President Mike Pence said he believes Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick “may need to go” following criticism over his handling of Nvidia’s sale of advanced AI technology to China and an alleged honey trapping scheme targeting the firm’s former CEO, Jensen Huang.

Appearing on CNN’s “The Source” Tuesday, host Kaitlan Collins asked Pence on President Trump’s defense of Huang — the Nvidia co-founder who resigned from company leadership last week after reports suggested he had an affair with a Chinese spy.

“Well, Jensen Huang had to go, and he needs to stay gone,” Pence said. “I mean, the fact that Nvidia had engaged in the transfer of our most sensitive semiconductor technology to carve-out companies that we now believe were transferring that to communist China is just totally unacceptable.”

The former vice president also called for an investigation into how Nvidia was “able to transfer our most advanced semiconductor technology to companies doing business with China.”

Lutnick is accused of withholding sanctions against Megaspeed, the Singapore-based tech company at the center of Huang’s resignation. The ex-CEO departed Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with one of the Singaporean company’s former executives, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence suspected of espionage and accused of smuggling AI chips to China.

When asked if Lutnick needed to depart his post, Pence replied, “Well, I think we’ll get to the bottom of it, and he may need to go.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also pointed the finger at Lutnick for holding back sanctions against Megaspeed, while lawmakers are concerned the tech firm exploited a loophole allowing Chinese clients to access Nvidia’s AI chips through data centers located in southeast Asia. 

When asked about why Lutnick allegedly delayed export controls for certain AI chips, Pence said he didn’t “understand why the export controls were loosened to begin with.”

GOP and Democratic lawmakers are leading efforts in both chambers to investigate Lutnick’s alleged involvement in the scandal. 

Lawmakers reportedly sent a letter to Brandon Lutnick, the commerce secretary’s son, who is the chairman of Canton Fitzgerald, a company with stockholdings with Nvidia, as part of its investigation push, according to The New York Times. The correspondence raised questions about Brandon Lutnick’s involvement with the firm’s investments into southeast Asian data centers.

data.title: US missed the climate change summit, but it can still lead on 35-by-35 goal
data.description:
Most countries in the world are meeting in Turkey for an annual climate change summit. In lieu of the often unrealistic and unmet emissions reduction targets discussed at these events, the theme of this conference is electrification — specifically, a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of global final energy demand to 35 percent by 2035, a fourfold acceleration of the current pace.

The U.S. did not send a delegation to the conference, and that’s too bad because we could win at this. And we could do it in a way that solves our data center problem.

Democratic and Republican voters both spoke on Nov. 3. They want change. They want cheaper energy and guardrails on data centers. In fact, if data centers had been a candidate, they would have been utterly smoked in the election. Forty-one states had data center restrictions or moratoria on the ballot and all but one passed. Data centers — and voter opposition to them — are thought to have had a significant role to play in Democratic pick-ups in Ohio and Texas.

But the reality is, given our love of the AI tools that make our lives easier and maybe just a little more fun, it seems clear that AI is here to stay. It’s either going to kill the planet or save us from ourselves. The U.S. can steer which direction this goes. It would be irresponsible of the U.S. to cede the entire AI industry to China, which is already eating our lunch in the clean energy race. Instead of throwing the baby out with the data center bathwater, we need to rethink how we build and operate data centers and how we steward responsible applications of AI.

This is our Sputnik 2.0 moment — except that instead of overtaking the Soviet Union and beating them to the moon, we make data centers palatable, AI safer, electrify the grid, and reduce our carbon emissions in the process.

If we required data center developers to power their facilities with clean energy, recycle the water, control the noise, and choose sites with robust setbacks, then we could address the fears of energy price spikes by putting responsibility of power usage on data center developers.

In directing how data centers are powered, we can also spur the nuclear revolution. Similar to the way that Operation Warp Speed provided for the development of Covid vaccines, we see a path for the government purchase or guarantees of the first, small nuclear reactors. Republican lawmakers and voters of all stripes should support such an investment.

We can and should invest in battery technology to hold all the power that the U.S. is capable of generating from solar power, wind power and geothermal sources. As I heard from a recently retired Air Force officer over the summer, “National security used to be about F-16s. Now it’s about who has the best battery. The country with the best battery wins.”

These ideas might be the beginning of a Republican rethink that shows us to be a party that cares about people and the places where they live, that boosts our economy, taps into our ingenuity, and puts us in a position of primacy. While the U.S. is absent from COP-31, we don’t have to be absent from the 35-by-35 goal. We can do our part to ensure that goal is not only achieved, but exceeded.

While I personally still believe that a revenue neutral, border adjustable carbon tax is the best way to fix the economics and solve climate change, in a tax-averse society, it’s a hard sell. But focusing on electrification and adopting a can-do spirit that is forward thinking feels in line with what voters demanded with their choices on Nov. 3.

This is our chance to not let those voters down.

Former U.S. Rep. Bob Inglis (R-S.C.) served in the U.S. House from 1993 to 1999 and from 2005 to 2011. He directs republicEn.org, a growing group of conservatives seeking free enterprise solutions to climate change.
